courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
md: Patches end a bug; detections outlive it. Word starting msdt.exe was abnormal before May 2022 and is still abnormal now, so the behaviour rule keeps catching the next abuse of a protocol handler.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Never use one keystream twice. Reusing keystream material across files turns any file whose original you hold into a key for others. Sound designs encrypt each file with its own key from a proper cipher and protect the master secret with public-key encryption.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
md: A full compromise of a hardened platform is a chain, usually renderer RCE plus sandbox escape plus kernel bug. Each extra wall forces another 0-day, and each stage is a separate chance to detect or break the attack.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Running a purple team exercise
md: A purple team exercise is a loop per technique: context, expectation, execution, investigation, fix, retest, record. The output is not a list of what the red team achieved but a list of what the blue team can now see that it could not see in the morning.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
md: Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The lethal trifecta and excessive agency
md: "Read-only" tools are not harmless in a trifecta. A tool that only fetches URLs is a perfect exit: the data goes out in the request.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: MCP and agent tools: when tool descriptions are the attack
md: Every MCP server you add is code you run and text your model obeys. Install few, from publishers you trust; pin and review their descriptions; show full arguments on approval; sandbox local servers; and do not combine private-data tools, untrusted-content tools and outbound tools in one agent.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
md: Each second-generation scheme buys one property with another: exact distributions with model-dependent tests or zero robustness gains, paraphrase robustness with slow rejection sampling, code detection with model access, user ids with more text, public verification with long outputs. Pick the property your use case cannot live without.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Validation is a fixed checklist the receiver owns: pinned algorithm, trusted issuer's key, signature, iss, aud, exp and nbf with small leeway, type. A library helps only when you pass it every one of those rules.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report. You will also meet BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model), which describes what real companies' programmes do rather than prescribing a target.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
md: Finding bugs is linear work; removing bug classes compounds. A mature programme spends part of its budget on defaults, paved roads and language choices that make the next thousand findings never happen.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes (4xx codes such as 400 Bad Request mean the request itself is wrong, so it fails the same way again), billing or quota errors.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
md: Forced periodic rotation makes passwords weaker, not stronger: people make the smallest possible change. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider (a cybercriminal group that targets companies through their IT help desks, lesson 12) repeats NIST's advice to refrain from recurring password changes. Change on evidence of compromise instead.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
md: Identity attacks leave traces in authentication logs: failures, travel, new devices, MFA changes. Centralising login through SSO makes those traces easy to collect, and makes the IdP the account to protect most.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: `inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Reading decompiler output critically
md: A decompiler's output is a hypothesis built from guesses about functions, conventions and types. Each fix you make (define a function, set a signature, apply a struct) removes a guess, and the output improves everywhere that information flows.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 matched an FP32 reference token for token 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's own ternary formats TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
md: Agner Fog's rule of thumb: a conditional jump beats a conditional move when the code is part of a dependency chain and prediction is better than about 75 percent. For random binary-search keys (about 50 percent) cmov wins; for keys that cluster, the branch wins.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: Do not let IT set the MTD by asking "how fast could we restore it?". That gives you the current capability, not the requirement. The BIA asks the process owner "how long until this becomes unacceptable?", and the gap between the two answers is the work of the rest of this course.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Granularity is a recovery requirement. In multi-tenant systems (one data store, many customers), "restore the database" also rolls back every unaffected customer. Write RTOs per restore size (one record, one tenant, many tenants, everything) and test each, because they are different procedures with very different times.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model
md: A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: Misconception: "filler tokens did not help, so all of a model's reasoning must be in the words." Lanham's result shows that particular models did not learn to use filler. Pfau et al. show training can teach a transformer to compute across meaningless tokens on suitable problems, and nothing in a monitor's view of "......" would reveal what was computed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: These methods sit uneasily with "keep optimization pressure off the CoT". VFT trains directly on CoT content. The difference from Baker et al.'s failure is direction and timing: it rewards saying more, before RL, and the RL reward never reads the CoT. VFT was tested on one 8B model with multiple-choice cues; whether it holds for frontier agents is open.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Signature nonces: reuse, weak randomness and deterministic signing
md: Two identical signatures of the same message are harmless with RFC 6979. The alarm is the same r value on two different messages under one key: that means k repeated, and the private key must be considered public.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order: remapping launch indices to tile coordinates so that CTAs running at the same time cover a compact patch of tiles rather than one long row) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: "It was public, so it was allowed" is the most common mistake. The ACM Code of Ethics says it directly: "A system being publicly accessible is not sufficient grounds on its own to imply authorization." Lesson 4 shows the opposite mistake too: officials calling ordinary viewing of a public page a crime.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: CMA: s1 knowingly unauthorised access attempt (2 years); s2 with intent to commit a further offence (5); s3 unauthorised impairment (10); s3ZA serious damage (14 or life); s3A tools for those offences (2). Authorisation must come from someone entitled to control that kind of access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: Wassenaar (2013, amended 2017) controls intrusion software platforms and development technology, with carve-outs for vulnerability disclosure and incident response. The US implements it through BIS's 2021 rule and License Exception ACE; destination, end user and intended unauthorised use decide when a licence is needed.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: When the problem is your own organisation: record the facts, escalate internally to the top, take legal advice, and use lawful external channels (regulators, law enforcement) if ignored. Never relabel a breach, pay for silence, or mislead an investigator.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
md: Regression methods learn mixture to loss from many cheap runs and search the fit. They work when the fitted function has the right shape and accurate parameters: a linear fit picks a corner, and mis-set laws can lose to uniform weights. Always compare against stratified sampling, and judge data choices with small models scored on continuous metrics.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Deleting the primary copy is not deletion. Exports, tickets, caches, logs and backups each need their own retention, and backups usually expire last. Lesson 13 shows a way to make old backups unreadable all at once: encrypt them and destroy the key.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
md: Every exception is a hole. Allowlisting a whole team, a whole domain or a whole application because one rule was noisy removes protection from every future leak through that path. Fix the detector, then make narrow, reviewed exceptions with an expiry date.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
md: Internet-facing honeypots produce intelligence, internal decoys produce alerts. Never page someone for a hit on an Internet honeypot; feed its data into enrichment and blocklists instead.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
md: Judge deception by evidence: decoys placed on attack paths, tested regularly, alerts that reach a person fast and are mostly real, and at least one detection you would otherwise have missed.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
md: The question to ask of every part of a pipeline: who can change what this runs, and what can it reach when it does? If the answer to the first is "anyone who can open a PR" and to the second is "production", there is a gap, however many scanners run.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
md: A VSN changes when a volume is reformatted and is only 32 bits on FAT, so a match is strong corroboration, not a unique fingerprint. Combine it with the device serial and times. The meanings of the 0x64 to 0x67 properties also vary by Windows build: test on a reference system before testifying to them.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: Response length growth during RL is partly an optimizer artifact. Check the loss normalization (a constant normalizer as in Dr. GRPO, $\lambda < 1$ for PPO) and the mix of solvable problems before adding a length penalty, and log length separately for correct and incorrect rollouts.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: The modes are far apart on hard problems. Qwen3-235B-A22B scored 85.7 on AIME 2024 thinking and 40.1 without. Fusion also had a price: for Qwen3-32B, thinking-mode AIME 2024 fell from 83.8 to 81.4 after the fusion and general-RL stages. A user-chosen switch is only as good as the user's guess about difficulty.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
md: UAX #15: "Normalization Forms KC and KD must not be blindly applied to arbitrary text", because they erase distinctions that can matter. Use NFKC (usually with case folding, next lesson) for identifiers such as usernames, and NFC for stored text you will show back to people.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees
md: For every structured format: one strict parser at the boundary, reject anything ambiguous (duplicate fields, malformed headers, unknown XML structure), and pass the parsed result, not the original bytes, to the rest of the system.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
md: Misconception: "a GrantedAccess of 0x1FFFFF on LSASS is always an attack." Security products, backup agents and admin tools often request all access. Context decides: which signed program, how often, from which path, and with which call trace. Baseline the normal requesters on your hosts, then alert on the rest.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: A service principal can hold an Entra admin role, and Microsoft names those that do as control plane assets. An app with Global Administrator, or with permission to assign roles, is a Global Administrator that has no MFA prompt to bypass. Review apps in role assignments with the same care as people.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Misconception: resetting a compromised user's password ends the attacker's access immediately. It revokes only refresh tokens obtained with the password (revoke sessions for the rest), and an access token already issued keeps working until it expires (up to 90 minutes) at any service that does not support CAE, and app sessions with their own cookies (the federation course's offboarding gap) are untouched.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: Misconception: 'We have Conditional Access requiring MFA, so password spraying is solved.' Only for accounts and flows the policies cover. Excluded service accounts, legacy protocols if not blocked, and service principals with secrets all sit outside it, and attackers spray exactly those.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
md: Baseline: few cloud-only admins on passkeys through PIM, restricted consent and reviewed apps, legacy auth and device code blocked, device-bound tokens where possible, hybrid bridges as Tier 0, and every log exported. Runbook: contain identities, hunt persistence in apps, devices and federation, scope data, evict at the root.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Refinement says nothing about the steps the mapping hides. If the mapping ignores a variable that matters (say, durable state on disk), a wrong design can still refine the spec. Review the mapping as carefully as the spec.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
md: A fake quantizer reproduces a format's numerics, not its speed: what each value becomes after casting and scaling. Real hardware adds its own accumulation precision and order, so validate surprising results on the target GPU, but use the fake quantizer to test a recipe on your own tensors first.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Single signals are weak: IPs can be rented, fingerprints spoofed. Value comes from combining them and from relationships: the same device across many accounts, or claims that contradict each other.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
md: Never log, store or send card numbers through your own analytics, logs or support tools to "help fraud analysis". Work with your provider's card fingerprint instead: it links repeat use of a card without bringing the card data into PCI DSS scope.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
md: "Fraud went down" can mean the control worked, the attackers moved elsewhere, or labels have not arrived yet. Always read loss together with friction (approval rate, insult rate) and with label maturity.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
md: A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
md: A trip runs on date D if its service_id is active on service day D. Its times are offsets from noon minus 12 hours on D, may exceed 24:00:00, and are in agency_timezone. Anything you compute from the schedule must keep the pair (trip_id, service date), not just trip_id.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: A 75-cent gap and the Morris worm: the 1980s internet learns
md: 1980s lessons that still hold: reconcile records that should agree; plant decoys that only an intruder would touch; and when something spreads, close the entry points rather than chasing copies. The worm also produced an institution, CERT/CC, which is why there is now a neutral place to report vulnerabilities.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: 2010: Operation Aurora and Stuxnet bring state operations into view
md: "It came from a nation state, so nothing could have stopped it" is a common excuse. Aurora still needed an unpatched browser and a flat internal network; Stuxnet most likely relied on removable media to reach isolated engineering computers. Sophisticated attackers raise the bar for detection, but basic controls still remove paths.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: MOVEit and xz: mass extortion and the backdoor that almost shipped
md: "Open source is safe because many eyes review it" did not hold: the trigger was only in release tarballs, which few people compare against git, and the payload hid in binary test files. It was caught by one engineer chasing a performance anomaly, not by review.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: Misconception: "adding a random delay hides the timing". Noise only forces the attacker to average more measurements; Paul Kocher showed in 1996 that the number of measurements grows with the square of the noise (lesson 2). Remove the dependency instead.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Where an HTTP/1.1 message ends: Content-Length and chunked
md: Python's own number parsing is lenient: `int('0x5', 16)` and `int('+5')` both return 5, and `int('1_0', 16)` returns 16 because underscores are allowed. That is why the parser checks that a chunk size contains only hex digits and Content-Length only decimal digits **before** converting. Two servers that both "parse numbers" can still disagree about which strings are numbers.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Poisoning with errors and with normalisation
md: Cache and origin must agree on two things: which requests are errors, and which URLs are the same resource. Make the cache stricter than the origin on input, and make its key normalisation match how the origin routes.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: The synchronous stall is the classic THP latency spike. `/proc/vmstat` counts it: `compact_stall` increments every time a process stalls to run compaction, with `compact_success` and `compact_fail` alongside. A rising `compact_stall` next to tail-latency spikes is a strong hint. Tail latency is the time of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile, called p99.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
md: A recurrent state is compact but not divisible. Every serving feature that cuts a cache at an arbitrary token (sharing a prefix, rejecting speculative tokens, pausing a prefill) needs a saved state at that exact position or a recomputation from an earlier one. Plan where states are checkpointed the way you plan KV memory.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
md: Common misconception: HyDE shows the user the generated passage. It does not. The hypothetical document only becomes a vector; everything returned is a real document from the corpus. Hallucinations (fluent but false details) can still hurt, but by moving the vector, not by being displayed.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
md: Encryption alone would not fix this. If any host can still connect and is trusted once connected, encrypting the write just hides the attack from your monitor. What is missing is authentication and authorisation of the sender, which Modbus/TCP Security adds (lesson 7).

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: Segment so that the office cannot reach the controllers, pass data out through a DMZ (one way where possible), let in remote support only through an approved, timed, MFA-protected door, and keep the safety system off every routed path.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
md: Do not write this yourself for production. Use a maintained SAML library, configure it strictly (signed assertions required, exact Audience and ACS URL, no IdP-initiated login unless needed) and patch it quickly: lesson 7 is about a widely used library that had a critical flaw in step 5. The toy here exists to make each check visible.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
md: A valid signature proves possession of a key, not that the IdP made a decision. Once the key or the trust list is in an attacker's hands, every SP check passes, so defence moves to protecting the IdP like a domain controller and to correlating SP logins with IdP issuance.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Access reviews and certification: asking again, and meaning it
md: A completed review is not the same as a working control. 100% approved in two seconds per item is evidence that a form was filled in.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Why change detection must align images first
md: Alignment comes before differencing, always. Without it, the change mask mostly measures camera motion, concentrated on every edge in the image.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: Declaring is a decision with consequences: it starts the plan, assigns an incident commander and may start legal clocks. Write the criteria down beforehand so that nobody has to be brave at 2 a.m.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Windows artefacts: event logs, Prefetch, Amcache, Shimcache, MFT
md: A Shimcache or Amcache entry alone does not prove the program ran. Mandiant showed Shimcache entries created just by browsing a folder on some Windows versions. Look for corroboration: Prefetch, 4688, Sysmon, EDR telemetry.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection
md: The fix for every injection is the same idea: keep code and data in **separate channels**, so the interpreter never has to guess which is which. For SQL that is a parameterised query, for the shell an argument list, for templates a template variable. Escaping and filtering are fallbacks for when no separate channel exists.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
md: If the tail update becomes visible before the SQE fields, the kernel can read a half-written request (say, the right opcode with a stale fd). This is a real bug class in hand-rolled ring code. liburing (Axboe's helper library, lesson 3) does the barriers for you, which is the main reason to use it even if you want raw control elsewhere.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Default passwords: Mirai from the maker's side
md: Lockouts can become a denial-of-service tool: an attacker can lock the real owner out by failing on purpose. ETSI notes this tension. Prefer increasing delays per source over hard account lockouts, and never lock out local recovery (a reset button that requires physical presence).

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: A secure device end to end, and where to practise
md: Secure devices come from a few decisions made early and kept: nothing shared across units, nothing runs unless signed, nothing listens unless needed, every unit can be updated and the update cannot go backwards, and someone is responsible for bugs until a published end date.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: eval, new Function and why node:vm is not a sandbox
md: Inside one process, JavaScript objects are a graph, and any shared object is a path back to the host. node:vm, vm2 and similar tools are useful for running *your own* code in a clean global, never for running someone else's. Untrusted code needs a process, container or VM boundary.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle is sound but not complete: everything it reports is real, but it can miss anomalies. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms, rows matching a WHERE clause that appear or vanish between two reads in one transaction) are outside its analysis.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Treat distillation as function matching: same input to teacher and student every step, as many distinct inputs as you can generate, and a schedule far longer than supervised training. Judge the run against a same-size model trained on labels, and track agreement with the teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Coconut reached 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4. The probes suggest deferring commitment is part of why, but staged training without any thoughts also reached 95.5%.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
md: Do not mix the two limits up. A bigger state helps recall but does nothing for parity: with eigenvalues in [0, 1], even a huge state fails at long lengths. Negative eigenvalues fix parity but add no storage. Production models answer the recall limit by keeping some attention layers (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
md: Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
md: Use lockdown integrity mode on fleets that run eBPF or kprobe sensors; confidentiality also blocks the reads those sensors need. Lockdown only ever goes up until reboot. For sysctl, the last-sorted file wins across directories, so always verify running values, not config files.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: A kprobe policy depends on a kernel function name and its arguments, which are not a stable interface and can change between kernel versions. Test policies against every kernel version in your fleet, and watch for the policy failing to load after a kernel update.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
md: Fleet response = package-aware inventory, immediate exposure reduction through config management, ring rollout with restarts, verification of running code, and detection of the attack's noise in the meantime. Never triage on upstream version strings alone.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
md: QLoRA separates a storage type (NF4, 4 bits) from a compute type (BF16). Only the adapters are trained, so quantization error in the frozen base can be compensated by the adapters, and memory drops by about 4x versus a 16-bit base.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Code signing: what a signature on a Mac proves
md: A valid signature says *who* built the code and that it is unchanged. It does not say the code is safe. Attackers sign malware with Developer ID certificates obtained under real or stolen identities, and in the 3CX case (lesson 17) the vendor's own build system signed the trojanised app.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Hunting across a fleet: osquery tables and detection logic
md: Mac fleets are full of developers who run curl, shells and unsigned tools all day. Rules that fire on "osascript ran" drown a SOC. Anchor detections on combinations and ancestry (browser to Terminal to curl to osascript to dscl) and on things legitimate tools rarely do (validating a user's password from a script).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
md: Malware can notice it is in a VM and change behaviour (ATT&CK calls this Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, T1497). An empty or 'boring' run does not prove a file is benign; it may prove only that the sample saw your lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: C2 detection rests on things the operator finds hard to change: timing patterns, the process making the connection, rare destinations, and on-host artifacts. Fortra's own guide shows the traffic shape can be reconfigured (Malleable C2 profiles let an operator change how Beacon's HTTP traffic looks), so content signatures alone age quickly.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why Matryoshka prefixes are safe for shortlisting.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Context parallelism: balanced causal splits and the KV ring
md: `a2a` splits heads, so Transformer Engine requires the number of query heads **and** of KV heads on each GPU to be divisible by CP. TP has already divided the heads: with 8 KV heads and TP = 4 each GPU holds 2, so a2a works for CP = 2 but is rejected for CP = 4. The p2p ring has no head constraint, which is one reason it is the default.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: What only RAM knows: Duqu 2.0 and the case for memory
md: Memory-resident code trades persistence for stealth. The defender's answer is to capture memory before anyone reboots, restarts a service or "cleans" the host, and to treat the image as the only copy of that evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it
md: Scope by exposure, not only by proof of theft. Every account with a session or cached logon on a compromised host goes on the reset list. Memory adds who touched LSASS and how, which tells you whether the attacker could also have reached accounts that were not logged on.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Off-by-one: a single byte too far
md: Off-by-one bugs live at the boundary. A test suite that tries length n - 1, n and n + 1 for every buffer finds most of them; AddressSanitizer turns the silent one-byte write into a loud error.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: A triplet only produces gradient when the negative is inside d(a,p) + m. Mining decides which of those active triplets you spend compute on.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
